candidates.premise: GPU prefill saturation and tile quantization depend on matrix dimensions, tensor-parallel degree, kernel implementation, and hardware; a saturation point measured on one configuration is not universal.

candidates.headline: Stall-free batching does not imply or guarantee throughput gains when decode batches become compute-bound.
candidates.claim: Stall-free batching's throughput benefit depends on decode memory-bound slack; when decode batches become compute-bound, the mechanism does not guarantee the same throughput gain and may require a smaller token budget.
candidates.paper_fact: When the number of tokens is small, execution time is dictated by the cost of fetching weights from HBM memory. Hence, execution time is largely stagnant in the 128-512 tokens range, especially for higher tensor parallel degrees. Once the number of tokens in the batch cross a critical threshold, the operation become compute bound and the runtime increases linearly with number of tokens.
candidates.premise: Packing extra tokens into a batch only has low marginal latency while the batch is memory-bound; once compute-bound, added tokens increase iteration time roughly linearly.
candidates.inference: Because the paper shows linear-layer time is flat only up to a token threshold and then linear, the stall-free slack is workload- and scale-dependent; at high batch/context the mechanism's net throughput benefit can shrink.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): at batch size 64 and long context, the decode batch crosses the compute-bound threshold; adding a prefill chunk increases iteration time roughly linearly, so the same token budget yields less TBT headroom.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If context lengths grow or batch sizes rise until decodes become compute-bound, the token budget must shrink or TBT SLOs will be violated, reducing the throughput advantage.
candidates.critical_link: Decode memory-bound slack -> ability to co-run prefill chunks with little TBT impact; if decode becomes compute-bound, that link weakens.
necessary_conditions: Decode batches remain in the memory-bound regime.
Token budget stays below the compute-bound threshold for the model/hardware/parallelism.
Prefill chunks can fill leftover budget without pushing iteration latency past SLO.
defeaters: Hardware/software changes that increase the compute-bound threshold or memory bandwidth.
Smaller batch sizes or shorter contexts that preserve decode slack.
Disaggregated prefill/decode that avoids co-running interference.
do_not_infer: Do not infer stall-free batching has no throughput benefit at scale.
Do not infer the paper ignores compute-bound behavior; it reports the threshold.
Do not infer all workloads become compute-bound.

candidates.headline: Decode-prioritizing request-level batching does not guarantee low TBT under all loads or workloads

candidates.premise: TBT is the interval between consecutive output tokens for a request; it can be affected by scheduling, but system load, admission delay, and batch completion also affect user-visible latency and capacity.
candidates.inference: The paper's TBT benefit is conditional on admitted decodes not being interrupted by prefills. It is not a guarantee that TBT remains low for all requests or that the system meets latency SLOs under high load or length variance.

candidates.conditional_consequence: If load is low and TBT is the strict objective, decode-prioritizing can be safe; if load rises or request lengths vary, throughput loss and queueing can dominate and TBT alone does not ensure SLO satisfaction.
candidates.critical_link: The mechanism removes prefill interference for ongoing decodes, but TBT optimization is a proxy for one latency metric, not a guarantee of end-to-end latency or capacity.
